titre: Translating a contract under Swiss law: what legal multilingualism changes
extrait: Federal acts exist in German, French and Italian, and all three versions are equally authoritative. What this means in practice for a contract: abbreviations that change with the language, an English translation with no legal force, false friends between Swiss Italian and the Italian of Italy, and a three-minute method for checking a term.
bref: In Switzerland, the terminology of a contract is not a matter of style. Federal acts are published in German, French and Italian, and all three versions are equally authoritative. English is not one of them. A translator therefore does not look for an equivalent: they find the term the legislature has already chosen.

titre: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, pitches at EPFL Investor Day 2024
extrait: Three minutes on stage and an unexpected tip from a pitch masterclass: cut the team slide. Paula Reichenberg applied it that same afternoon, for a more relaxed and, hopefully, more convincing pitch.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, pitched at EPFL Investor Day, the largest investor meet-up in French-speaking Switzerland. Before taking the stage, she attended a pitch masterclass led by Jordi Montserrat. One tip took her by surprise: cut the team slide, because the energy you bring on stage counts for more.
title: Paula Reichenberg at EPFL Investor Day 2024 · Neur.on
description: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, pitched at EPFL Investor Day, the largest investor meet-up in French-speaking Switzerland, with an unexpected tip in mind.
court: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, pitches at EPFL Investor Day 2024
corps:
What should you cut from your pitch deck when you only have three minutes on stage?

Before taking the stage, all participants were invited to a pitch masterclass led by one of the brightest minds in the field, Jordi Montserrat.

One of his remarks really took Paula by surprise. The discussion was about what to cut from a pitch that does not fit the time allowed. The general view was that the five-year roadmap or the financials could fairly go.

But Jordi said: cut the team.

The team? The backbone of the company in terms of expertise and personality? No way that would fly with potential investors.

But Jordi’s reasoning was crystal clear: “When you’re on stage, you’re representing the vibe of your company. If that’s good, it’s worth more than the team slide.”

And you know what? Paula applied the advice to her pitch that afternoon. It gave her two or three more breathers, for a more relaxed and (hopefully) more convincing presentation.

She knows full well that she is not abandoning her team. After all, in front of interested investors, it never takes her three minutes to start raving about her co-founders and team anyway.

titre: Key takeaways from the LegalTechTalk 2024 conference in London
extrait: “I refuse to pay for information I already have.” General counsel and law firms compared their views on trust, efficiency and the place of technology in legal services.
bref: Neur.on reports on the discussions at the LegalTechTalk 2024 conference in London. General counsel argued for a relationship of trust and knowledge sharing with their external law firms. Law firms highlighted bespoke teams, data-driven process analysis and their role as technology advisers, including in legal translation.
title: LegalTechTalk 2024 in London: key takeaways · Neur.on
description: Neur.on shares its takeaways from LegalTechTalk 2024 in London: what general counsel expect, building trust with law firms and the role of LegalTech.
court: Key takeaways from the LegalTechTalk 2024 conference in London
corps:
What do general counsel expect from their law firms?

“I refuse to pay for information I already have,” exclaims the general counsel of an energy company, when asked about his top criteria for appointing external law firms.

“This is a simplistic view and certainly no solid basis for building a long-term, fruitful relationship with panel law firms,” retorts the general counsel of a multinational, responsible for managing the legal functions of more than 15 countries. “If you expect a law firm to add value and provide actionable business advice, in-house lawyers and external counsel must share knowledge and build common ground. This requires investment and trust from both sides.”

“‘Trusting’ is not the first adjective that comes to mind when describing lawyers: they have been trained to stay on their guard and to be sceptical, to better protect their clients. Making the switch does not come easy,” responds a legal innovation officer at a corporate law firm.

“They must understand that general counsel do not always expect guaranteed correctness: receiving their best-informed opinion in urgent matters is the priority, and forecasts that turn out to be wrong are part of business life. Giving your panel law firms clear guidance on the type and amount of work they can expect from your company also helps build trust: if the lawyers can invest enough in understanding your company and your expectations, they will proactively suggest ways to work more efficiently.”

How are law firms organising themselves to respond?

“When working with general counsel, our lawyers’ objective is to act as an extension of their team,” confirms the head of innovation at a law firm in continental Europe. “Our first focus when onboarding a new client is to find counterparts whose working and communication style matches that of the general counsel. To tackle each of their issues, we then set up ad hoc teams with the right mix of field expertise, educational background and levels of seniority.”

Why is technology becoming a law firm deliverable?

“In addition to the right team, data-driven process analysis is key to delivering legal services efficiently,” adds Jordan Lee, Chief Strategy Officer of Pogust Goodhead, a law firm specialising in collective redress. “Once you identify a step that can be automated, or repetitive patterns that can be streamlined, the tech team can step in and capture even the smallest marginal gains. These quickly add up to substantial cost savings and higher quality.”

“There is a clear trend: clients expect their lawyers to also act as technology advisers whenever legal processes can be optimised. For example, in Neur.on’s field of expertise, any client facing major translation challenges in a legal case expects their lawyers to have a cost-efficient and secure solution ready. Testing, benchmarking and co-creating LegalTech tools have become part of what law firms deliver.”

These are a few takeaways from the conference. Mark your calendars for next year’s edition! A big thank you to Bradley Collins, Charlotte Johnstone and Merlin Beyts for the brilliant organisation.

titre: Should AI start-ups be scared of the AI Act? Lessons from the Grand Challenge
extrait: Eight AI solutions assessed against the draft AI Act: Neur.on draws three lessons, including a low-cost compliance lever for financially stretched start-ups.
bref: Representatives of Neur.on, iCoSys and CertX took part in the University of St Gallen’s first Grand Challenge on the EU AI Act. They assessed the compliance of eight AI solutions with the draft regulation. According to Neur.on, awareness of AI risks and a culture of compliance add a great deal of value without major expense.
title: AI Act Grand Challenge: should start-ups worry? · Neur.on
description: In 2023, Neur.on, iCoSys and CertX assessed eight AI solutions against the draft EU AI Act at the University of St Gallen’s first Grand Challenge.
court: Should AI start-ups be scared of the AI Act? Lessons from the Grand Challenge
corps:
What was the University of St Gallen Grand Challenge on the AI Act?

We were honoured to have representatives of Neur.on, iCoSys and CertX, along with other renowned AI specialists from around the world, take part in The First University of St. Gallen Grand Challenge: The EU AI ACT. During the event, we focused on assessing the compliance of eight advanced AI solutions with the current draft of the AI Act. These solutions covered robotics, process management and NLP analytics. Our diverse team brought together experts in machine learning, law and ISO 27001 certification.

Watch the report on the Swiss national TV news!

Should AI start-ups be scared of the AI Act?

Here are our key takeaways:

  • The fundamental principles of the EU AI Act (including human agency and oversight, technical robustness and safety, privacy and data governance, transparency, diversity, non-discrimination and fairness, and social and environmental impact) are well designed, deemed fair and essential for building widespread acceptance of, and trust in, artificial intelligence.
  • However, for financially stretched start-ups, complying with the requirements of the AI Act can feel like a sword of Damocles, consuming resources and slowing down development.
  • Fortunately, as we observed during the Grand Challenge, one aspect of compliance does not require significant expense yet adds tremendous value: AWARENESS of AI risks and a COMPANY CULTURE that prioritises compliance and responsible growth.

Let us work together towards an AI industry that embraces compliance, responsible development and a culture of trust.

Thank you to Thomas Burri for organising such a spectacular challenge, to SRF (Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen) for reporting on the event, and to all our team members: Jean Hennebert, Orane Laeri, Yael Iseli, Arman Iranfar and Marco Repetto Ph. D.

titre: Neur.on at the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne: the challenges of AI in legal translation
extrait: Why do tools like DeepL struggle with specialised legal and financial texts? At the GEN AI Summit 2024, Neur.on’s CEO discussed the nuances between legal systems, cultural barriers and the future of AI in translation.
bref: On 29 May 2024, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, spoke at the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne, in the “Domain Specific Innovation” session. She presented the limits of tools like DeepL for specialised legal and financial translation, the cultural and linguistic challenges of legal translation and the progress expected from AI in this field.
title: GEN AI Summit 2024 Lausanne: AI and translation · Neur.on
description: At the GEN AI Summit in Lausanne on 29 May 2024, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, spoke about the limits of machine translation for legal texts.
court: Neur.on at the GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne: the challenges of AI in legal translation
corps:
The GEN AI Summit 2024 in Lausanne brought together industry leaders and innovators to shape the future of technology. We are proud to share that our CEO, Paula Reichenberg, was one of the speakers at the summit on 29 May. She shared her insights into the dynamic world of generative AI.

At the summit, the discussions went beyond the major announcements from tech giants like OpenAI and Google. Participants were able to explore various use cases with panoramai.ch. These examples demonstrated the real value of generative AI and gave participants actionable insights for their own projects.

Paula took part in the “Domain Specific Innovation” session, alongside distinguished speakers such as Raphaël Briner, Pascal Wicht, Romain Rosay (CTO of Amplify) and Deepak Tewari (CEO of Privately). The session explored the nuances of AI and technology across different industries.

Key takeaways from Paula’s talk

  • Limitations of current machine translation tools: Paula highlighted the challenges of using tools like DeepL for specialised legal and financial translations. She stressed how difficult it is to render the nuances between different legal systems.
  • Cultural and linguistic challenges: She discussed the significant cultural and linguistic barriers to achieving accurate translations, which are critical in legal contexts.
  • Future aspirations for AI in legal translation: Paula presented the incremental improvements and future goals for AI to better serve the field of legal translation.

The broader impact of AI

The session also covered the wider effects of AI on society, including potential job losses and the ethical considerations of AI applications. Audience questions raised practical issues, such as the accuracy of age detection across different ethnic backgrounds and how to deal with deepfakes. The speakers reassured the audience about ongoing efforts to refine these technologies and make sure they meet regulatory standards.

court: Neur.on among the four finalists of the Swiss FinTech Awards 2024
corps:
Neur.on is one of the four finalists of the Swiss FinTech Awards 2024.

You think there has been a mix-up?

“But how could an AI-powered translation SaaS platform ever be considered a FinTech?” you might ask. Especially if you have met us at the countless LegalTech events we have taken part in.

Yet the jury of the Swiss FinTech Awards understands that accurate terminology and compelling wording go far beyond the legal domain.

For banks, precise language and powerful communication are the luxury packaging in which they deliver their expertise.

Imagine you receive a glossy brochure that is supposed to contain an insightful portfolio review from your private banker. You start reading. After only a few sentences, it is crystal clear that the whole thing has been machine-translated, and badly at that. The phrasing is off, the contextual inconsistencies pile up, and it is obvious to you that the end result has never even been reviewed by a native speaker.

Poor language inevitably instils a suspicion of incompetence and, perhaps even worse, of disrespect towards your readers. Unthinkable in the world of Swiss “financial haute horlogerie”.

Read more about the four finalists in Fintechnews Switzerland and Finanz und Wirtschaft.

Join us on 11 June at “FinTech 2024”, the flagship fintech conference organised by Finanz und Wirtschaft Forum at the GDI Gottlieb Duttweiler Institute in Rüschlikon, for an enthralling final.

titre: LegalTech and lawyers: allies or competitors? Lessons from the digital law firm day
extrait: Most LegalTech tools aim to serve lawyers, not to compete with them. Yet adoption remains difficult. A fit with working processes, an intuitive interface and responsive customer service: three keys to success.
bref: Neur.on’s founder took part in the LegalTech panel at the digital law firm day organised by the Conférence latine des bâtonniers on 29 September 2023. Her conclusion: the key to the success of a LegalTech tool is ease of use, with an intuitive interface, a fit with lawyers’ processes and responsive customer service.
title: LegalTech and lawyers: allies or competitors? · Neur.on
description: At the LegalTech panel of the Conférence latine des bâtonniers in 2023, the founder of Neur.on explains why ease of use matters more than anything else.
court: LegalTech and lawyers: allies or competitors? Lessons from the digital law firm day
corps:
Contrary to what some lawyers might fear, most of the LegalTech tools created in recent years aim to serve legal professionals rather than compete with them. Yet you hear as many LegalTech entrepreneurs disappointed by the reluctance with which their target audience greets their solutions as you hear lawyers complaining that the new tools offered to them do not fit their needs.

How can LegalTech start-ups and the legal professions be brought closer together?

The need to build a bridge between the innovative fervour of start-ups and the concrete needs of the legal professions led the Brussels Bar, under the leadership of Vinciane Gillet, to create a dedicated incubator. In Switzerland, we have to rely on the support of the Swiss LegalTech Association and on the commitment of a few pioneering law firms, which accept the responsibility of co-creating with LegalTech companies and invest the time and resources needed to test new tools (our thanks to them).

This was one of the topics discussed at the “LegalTech” panel of the digital law firm day organised by the Conférence latine des bâtonniers (Latin Conference of Bar Presidents), in which I had the pleasure of taking part alongside Vinciane Gillet (GILLET-LEX), Ariel Ben Hattar (Lenz & Staehelin) and Camille Auberson (Approovd).

What is the key to the success of a legal technology tool?

Asked by Juliette Ancelle (id est avocats) and Stéphanie Chuffart-Finsterwald (sigma legal) about the lessons I have learned as a LegalTech entrepreneur and founder of Neur.on, I would say that the key to the success of a legal technology tool is its ease of use. Lawyers’ packed schedules leave no room for technical training “in anticipation of a future need”. For example, since a law firm’s legal translation needs vary greatly from one year to the next, training assistants or trainees on a translation tool “out of context” would be a waste of time. Solutions must therefore be intuitive and logical enough for lawyers to get the result they expect the first time they use them, in a few clicks, or to call on responsive customer service that fills any knowledge gaps “ad hoc”.

To end with a rather easy pun, here is how a solution wins its case with lawyers:

  • a fit with lawyers’ working processes, with no ambition to change them;
  • an intuitive interface that requires no prior training;
  • customer service that adapts, including to the profession’s working hours and to emergencies.

titre: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, is part of UBS’s Female Founder Project 2025
extrait: Female founders do not get the same questions as male founders when raising funds. Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, chose to prepare with the UBS programme, and she hopes for some really tough questions.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, is part of UBS’s Female Founder Project 2025. The programme prepares female founders to meet investors. According to the Harvard Business Review, the questions put to women entrepreneurs focus mainly on risk, which can work against them. Paula Reichenberg therefore wants to come prepared.
title: Paula Reichenberg in the Female Founder Project 2025 · Neur.on
description: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, is part of UBS’s Female Founder Project 2025, a programme that prepares female founders to meet investors.
court: Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, is part of UBS’s Female Founder Project 2025
corps:
They say female founders get different questions. Our CEO Paula Reichenberg has different answers.

According to the Harvard Business Review, one of the many complex and mysterious reasons why women secure far less venture capital (1.8% of all venture capital in 2024) is the way questions are put to male and female founders during funding rounds.

Apparently, 67% of questions to male entrepreneurs are promotion-oriented (hopes, achievements, advancement), while 66% of questions to female entrepreneurs are prevention-oriented (safety, responsibility, potential risks).

What difference does that make? If you are not aware of these patterns, you inevitably answer in the motivational register of the question. For a woman, this can make her sound more conservative and more risk-averse, and so look like a less attractive investment opportunity.

Paula “doesn’t care” about being a woman. No more than she cares about her zodiac sign. She never complains that the world is unfair and does not waste time seeing herself as the victim of anything. She does the best she can with the cards she has been dealt.

But that means coming prepared, whether in a funding round or in any other business situation. Which is why she is grateful to UBS for including her in this year’s Female Founder programme. It is a modern approach to accelerating female founders’ success, through a holistic investor readiness programme.

She hopes this preparation will involve lots of really tricky questions.

titre: Geneva International Legal Week 2025: a panel on profitable AI with Paula Reichenberg
extrait: Are the up-front costs of AI just “training spend”? For anyone with a firm grasp of their budget, AI has to improve return on investment. In Geneva, a panel shares practical tips for using it profitably.
bref: Neur.on announced that its CEO, Paula Reichenberg, would speak on 12 March 2025 in a panel discussion at the Geneva International Legal Week (GILW25), held from 10 to 12 March by the Geneva International Legal Association. The panel was to give law firms and legal departments practical tips for using AI profitably.
title: GILW25: Paula Reichenberg on profitable AI · Neur.on
description: Neur.on announces that Paula Reichenberg will join a panel on using AI profitably at the Geneva International Legal Week on 12 March 2025.
court: Geneva International Legal Week 2025: a panel on profitable AI with Paula Reichenberg
corps:
Are the high up-front costs of integrating AI really just “training spend”?

At least that is what some innovation officers at early-adopter law firms and legal departments euphemistically call them.

But for anyone with a firm grasp of their budget, there has to be a clear sign that AI is adding to their return on investment.

You have probably heard it a hundred times over the past 24 months: using AI maximises your productivity, improves the quality of your work and reduces the risk of legal consequences and delays. It can also generate far more profit while making the justice system accessible to more people.

What you may not have heard is HOW to do it.

If that interests you, we cordially invite you to join our CEO at this year’s Geneva International Legal Week, organised by the Geneva International Legal Association (GILA). On 12 March, Paula Reichenberg will take part in a panel discussion starting at 10:45, alongside Karin Mülchi (Bridge Legal Group AG), Prof. Dr Vanessa Rüegger (University of Geneva) and Morgan Vallat (EY). The discussion will be moderated by Nicolas Torrent. Together, we will share our insights and practical tips for using AI profitably.

titre: Paula Reichenberg appointed to the HES-SO Strategy Council for 2025 to 2028
extrait: Planting trees so that future generations can harvest the fruit: Paula Reichenberg will sit on an HES-SO advisory body alongside figures from business, health, social work and culture.
bref: HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland has appointed Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, to its Strategy Council from 2025 to 2028. This advisory body brings together experts from academia, business, health, social work and culture. Paula Reichenberg intends to contribute to the education of future generations.

description: HES-SO has appointed Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, to its Strategy Council from 2025 to 2028, an advisory body with members from varied backgrounds.
court: Paula Reichenberg appointed to the HES-SO Strategy Council for 2025 to 2028
corps:
Planting trees so that future generations can harvest the fruit.

HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland has appointed our CEO Paula Reichenberg as a member of its Strategy Council from 2025 to 2028.

What is the HES-SO Strategy Council?

This advisory body brings together experts from varied backgrounds: academia, business, health, social work and culture. Its composition always reflects the fields studied at the university.

Why are universities of applied sciences essential to innovation in Switzerland?

Paula is honoured that HES-SO is giving her the opportunity to contribute to the education of future generations. Given the current geopolitical, societal and technological shifts, it is essential to future-proof Switzerland as an attractive playground and a thriving marketplace for start-ups and innovators.

EPFL and ETH Zurich work on deeptech and revolutionary technologies that make fundamental change possible. The role of schools of engineering and universities of applied sciences in Switzerland is just as fundamental: bringing technology from the lab to the market and winning over companies, listed corporations and SMEs alike, so that in the end the revolution reaches consumers and creates value for them.

As a mother of two, and chief executive and board member of several companies, Paula probably has little free time to spare.

Yet our CEO is convinced that having a say in the future of education will be energising, humbling and inspiring all at once. She will sit alongside expert figures, including:

  • Pascal Crittin, director of radio and television at SRF Schweizer Radio und Fernsehen;
  • Emilie Dellecker, director of HackGroup;
  • François Dubois, director of Pro Senectute Arc Jurassien;
  • Annina Grob, co-secretary of AVENIR SOCIAL;
  • Elisabeth Gutjahr, rector of the Mozarteum University Salzburg;
  • Olivier Haegeli, managing director of Willemin-Macodel and vice-president of the CCI du Jura;
  • Pierre-Henri Jaccaud, director of Skopia Art Contemporain, Geneva;
  • Christian Leumann, interim CEO of Inselspital, Bern;
  • Raphaëlle Luisier, group leader at the Idiap Research Institute;
  • Brigitte Rorive, president of the Hôpital Riviera-Chablais;

titre: LegalTechTalk 2024 in London: reinventing the law firm operating model
extrait: Why should law firms change their model, and how should they go about it? James Lane, Line Lolk Thomsen and Jordan Lee share their experience on a panel moderated by Paula Reichenberg.
bref: Neur.on announced that its CEO, Paula Reichenberg, would moderate a panel at LegalTechTalk 2024 in London on how law firms can rethink their operating models. James Lane (Stericycle), Line Lolk Thomsen (Plesner) and Jordan Lee (Pogust Goodhead) were to explain why and how to change in order to better serve general counsel.
title: LegalTechTalk 2024: reinventing law firms · Neur.on
description: At LegalTechTalk 2024 in London, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, moderates a panel on how law firms can rethink their operating models.
court: LegalTechTalk 2024 in London: reinventing the law firm operating model
corps:
Join us for an informative session on how law firms can rethink their operating models, with one goal: to better serve general counsel. Our panellists will explain WHY it is worth embracing change and HOW to implement it effectively.

Who are the panellists?

James Lane, Regional General Counsel at Stericycle, a global leader in medical waste and document destruction services, will share his extensive experience of working with panel law firms. Responsible for the legal function across Europe, the Middle East and Asia Pacific, James leads a cross-border legal team spanning more than a dozen countries. One of his first tasks at Stericycle was to set up an in-house legal function and conduct a comprehensive review of the panel law firms. James will outline his criteria for selecting the most efficient counsel and his strategy for building good working relationships.

Line Lolk Thomsen, Head of Projects and Innovation at Plesner, one of Denmark’s largest law firms, brings expertise from her background in innovation and business development. She holds a master’s degree from Copenhagen Business School and has worked in Latin America and Asia. Line now works at Plesner on areas such as process management and digitalisation. She will discuss how multidisciplinary teams, working together across disciplines, drive innovation.

Jordan Lee, Chief Strategy Officer at Pogust Goodhead, a pioneering collective redress law firm that operates on a “No-Win, No-Fee” model funded by hedge funds, will present practical use cases and examples illustrating the impact of their innovation-driven approach. Responsible for both demanding and driving innovation, Jordan will show how this model gains in speed and focus, ultimately improving case success rates and reducing costs.

Paula Reichenberg, Vice-President of the Swiss LegalTech Association and founder and CEO of Neur.on, will moderate the panel. Neur.on is the first LegalTech company to offer law firms, corporate legal departments and financial service providers a sector-specific platform for accurate legal and financial translations. In both capacities, Paula closely follows the growing expectations of law firms and legal departments regarding the efficiency gains that technology makes possible.

What topics will be covered?

The topics covered will include:

  • strategy-driven advice;
  • the value added by multidisciplinary teams;
  • client expectations regarding the use of LegalTech tools;
  • the benefits of data analytics in identifying potential efficiency gains.

Who is this session for?

This session is geared towards law firms that want to stay ahead in a competitive landscape. It offers an opportunity to gain insights from leaders at the forefront of legal innovation.

We are proud to highlight the remarkable career path of Orane Laeri, COO of Neur.on. The orientation.ch website has published an article about her, in which she describes her path in language sciences, linguistics and computational linguistics.

Orane’s academic journey led her to the University of Geneva, where she studied translation. Today, she stands out as head of operations at a dynamic LegalTech start-up specialising in neural machine translation.

Amid rapid advances in technology, Orane stresses that Neur.on’s objective is not to replace humans with machines, but to give them tailor-made tools. As she rightly points out: “There’s reason to rejoice: the machine is a tool that makes our work more interesting.”

Looking back on her first steps in professional life, Orane describes her journey from a legal translation internship to her current leadership role.

Her advice to students: embrace the fusion of technology and linguistics, and adapt to the way the profession is evolving. Whether you are drawn to the subtleties of language or to the connection between people and linguistics, there is a niche waiting to be mastered.

I invite you to find out more about Orane’s career by reading the full article.

titre: Commercial register of Schwyz: extracts translated into English by Neur.on’s AI
extrait: Every month, hundreds of people asked the commercial register of Schwyz for a reliable English translation of an extract. A look back at a project born in the Canton of Zurich’s Innovation Sandbox, and at the pitfalls of Swiss legal concepts.
bref: The commercial register of the canton of Schwyz offers AI translations of its extracts into English, something no other canton provides. Neur.on developed the translation model through the Canton of Zurich’s Innovation Sandbox for Artificial Intelligence. DV Bern AG, which is responsible for zefix.ch, handled implementation on the authorities’ side.
title: Schwyz commercial register extracts in English · Neur.on
description: Schwyz is the only canton whose commercial register offers AI translations of extracts into English, using a model developed by Neur.on.
court: Commercial register of Schwyz: extracts translated into English by Neur.on’s AI
corps:
The canton of Schwyz is an AI trendsetter.

The commercial register of Schwyz now offers something no other canton does: AI-powered translations of extracts into English.

Schwyz is not only the picturesque cradle of Switzerland, to which it gave its name. The canton has also just introduced a very pragmatic application of AI for the businesses based on its territory.

How did the extract translation project come about?

In the past, hundreds of people called the Schwyz commercial register every month with one and the same request: “I need a reliable English translation of an extract. Can you please help me?”

Othmar Aeschi of the Handelsregister Schwyz, known as a driver of innovation, had the informed intuition that AI could help. He got in touch with Raphael von Thiessen of the Business and Economic Development Division of the Amt für Wirtschaft, Kanton Zürich. Raphael featured the challenge in the office’s Innovation Sandbox for Artificial Intelligence and matched Neur.on with the Schwyz commercial register. And we developed the most accurate translation model for exactly this purpose. On the authorities’ side, the project was then implemented with the support of DV Bern AG, the specialist IT company responsible for the online commercial register platform, zefix.ch.

Why are Swiss legal concepts difficult to translate into English?

The challenge was not only one of natural language processing engineering. The even bigger question was how to translate typically Swiss legal concepts accurately into English, avoiding misunderstandings (or even awkwardness) in cross-border dealings.

  • Prokurist?
  • Kollektivunterschrift zu zweien?
  • Gesellschafter (einer GmbH vs. einer Kommanditgesellschaft)?
  • Streichung vs. Löschung?
  • Stimmrechtsaktien vs. Vorzugsaktien?

If you have ever wondered how to translate each of these terms correctly in context, you know how far off the mark a mediocre translation can be.

And to add some rainbow sprinkles to that lawyer-linguist sundae, we were also able to work on gender-neutral translations, especially for positions on the board of directors that, 50 years ago, were held exclusively by men.

As you can see, high-end AI projects require extensive human domain expertise to succeed.

Who contributed to the project?

A warm thank you to all the project stakeholders, in particular for the countless hours invested by Othmar Aeschi of the Handelsregister Schwyz, Raphael von Thiessen of the Amt für Wirtschaft, and Thierry Coita and Michael Gillmann of DV Bern AG. Thanks also to Carmen Walker Späh for her tireless support for Innovation Zurich.

Knowing the criteria jurors use to assess pitches can give you a competitive edge. Paula will assess the pitches based on Julia Maltby’s “10 Criteria for Investing in LegalTech”. Julia is an early-stage investor at Flybridge and X-Factor Ventures. Read her full list.

Here are three representative criteria out of these ten:

  1. Go beyond seat-based pricing: The legal market is hyper-fragmented, with many small practitioners. Innovative pricing models, such as taking a percentage of the savings generated, are more appealing than simple SaaS pricing.
  2. Avoid “black box” automation solutions: Lawyers need visibility into AI outputs and prefer a “human in the loop”, so that they can easily check facts and logic.
  3. 10x speed for non-billable tasks: Products that speed up non-billable legal functions are easier to sell, as they significantly improve productivity.

We hope these insights help you better understand how the jury evaluates pitches.

titre: Trust Valley 2023: cybersecurity and data sovereignty, a lasting Swiss tradition?
extrait: Legal translation projects are a weak and often overlooked link in data security. Invited by Trust Valley, Neur.on shares the lessons of a panel on SMEs and asks who will help fund a CHF 2.5 million Swiss sandbox.
bref: Neur.on took part in a panel at the Trust Valley day at EPFL’s Rolex Learning Center in 2023. The panel looked at the pressure that digital security puts on SMEs and start-ups. Neur.on relayed its clients’ request: a 100% Swiss infrastructure, not subject to the CLOUD Act, for testing generative AI.
title: Trust Valley 2023: Swiss data sovereignty · Neur.on
description: At the Trust Valley day 2023 at EPFL, Neur.on spoke about data security in SMEs and relayed the call for a 100% Swiss infrastructure for testing AI.
court: Trust Valley 2023: cybersecurity and data sovereignty, a lasting Swiss tradition?
corps:
The Trust Valley day at EPFL’s Rolex Learning Center brought together stakeholders from politics, academia, cybersecurity and the private sector, especially SMEs, to discuss the concrete challenges facing our country’s economy.

Neur.on serves Swiss law firms, banks and public administrations. It addresses one of their weakest links in terms of data security (yes, legal translation projects represent a significant but often overlooked risk!). Lennig Pedron therefore kindly invited us to share our experience as a LegalTech start-up that places digital security at the heart of its business.

What pressure does digital security put on SMEs?

Here are some key takeaways from the panel on the pressure faced by SMEs and start-ups:

  • High-level digital security demands substantial investment: infrastructure, processes, documentation and, above all, a matching corporate culture, shared at all levels and in all departments. The total often runs to a six-figure sum each year.
  • Law firms and other SMEs outside the ICT sector often lack the resources and expertise needed to properly assess their suppliers’ security levels. That leaves them no option but to “trust” or “hope for the best”.
  • Specialised ICT providers such as Neur.on can take responsibility for specific process steps, but overall knowledge and awareness remain with the SME.
  • Programmes and associations such as Trust4SMEs, the Swiss AI Center for SMEs of HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland and the Swiss LegalTech Association are there to help, with guides, white papers and training.

What are Swiss SMEs asking of the public sector?

However, the main message from our clients and from LegalTech stakeholders is addressed to the Swiss public sector and to innovation programmes:

Swiss SMEs and start-ups are eager to explore the potential of generative AI for their sector. To do so, they must be able to use their own data with LLMs without worrying about data leaks or uncontrolled data flows. They urgently request a 100% Swiss infrastructure, not subject to the US CLOUD Act or Patriot Act, to test different technologies securely.

Who is willing to help raise the CHF 2.5 million needed for a Swiss SME sandbox?

Is Switzerland ready to play a role in the digitalisation race?

Join Neur.on in its commitment to the security and success of Swiss businesses on this journey.

titre: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, named a “Digital Shaper 2023” by BILANZ
extrait: A distinction that belongs to the whole team. Neur.on takes the opportunity to restate three convictions about the digitalisation of law: technology that serves lawyers, transparency and human expertise.
bref: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, has been named a “Digital Shaper 2023” by BILANZ Wirtschaftsmagazin, digitalswitzerland, PME, HANDELSZEITUNG and Innosuisse. Neur.on credits the distinction to the commitment of its whole team. The company stands for a digitalisation of law that respects lawyers’ work, relies on transparency and values human expertise.
title: Paula Reichenberg named Digital Shaper 2023 · Neur.on
description: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, has been named a “Digital Shaper 2023” by BILANZ, digitalswitzerland, PME, HANDELSZEITUNG and Innosuisse.
court: Paula Reichenberg, CEO and founder of Neur.on, named a “Digital Shaper 2023” by BILANZ
corps:
This distinction is a testament to the remarkable dedication and collaborative spirit of the entire Neur.on team.

In the realm of “digital shaping”, success is the result of collective effort. This rings especially true in the legal sector, where the principles of Trust, Accuracy and Ethics take precedence over fleeting notions such as Profitability, Entrepreneurial Risk… and sometimes Innovation.

At Neur.on, we firmly believe that genuine digitalisation succeeds when:

  • Technology empowers without overpowering: our approach is to align technology smoothly with lawyers’ working methods and professional requirements. It is about harmonising innovation with the essence of legal practice, without imposing unnecessary change.
  • Transparency is the cornerstone: we hold the principle of transparency dear. We refrain from hollow boasting and instead give lawyers accurate information on the reliability of our results. Honest information enables them to make informed decisions.
  • Human expertise is strengthened: while technology is a powerful ally, it can never replace the depth and breadth of human expertise. We champion the role of lawyers, who know how to handle complexity, and we recognise that no algorithm can replicate their nuanced understanding of diverse situations.

Together, we are committed to reshaping our sector so that it brings joy to all its stakeholders.

titre: BDÜ conference 2022: Paula Reichenberg on collaboration between lawyers and translators
extrait: Good translations come from open communication between lawyers and translators. A look back at a panel discussion at the BDÜ conference, and at what each side expects of machine translation.
bref: In 2022, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, took part in a panel discussion at the BDÜ e.V. conference on working in and with law firms. She pointed out that lawyers expect translators not to deny the potential of machine translation, while translators would like lawyers not to overestimate it.
title: BDÜ conference 2022: lawyers and translators · Neur.on
description: In 2022, Paula Reichenberg, CEO of Neur.on, took part in a panel discussion at the BDÜ conference on working in and with law firms.
court: BDÜ conference 2022: Paula Reichenberg on collaboration between lawyers and translators
corps:
Paula Reichenberg, our CEO, had the privilege of taking part in a panel discussion on working in and with law firms at the conference of the BDÜ e.V. - die qualifizierten Dolmetscher und Übersetzer, alongside Karen Rückert and Dirk Poppendieck. The discussion was moderated by Richard Delaney.

Karen’s key takeaway from the panel discussion is this: “Good translations are the result of open communication between lawyers and translators. But this does not mean that lawyers should be mind readers. Translators need to be confident enough to ask the right questions to get the information they need to produce a translation which is fit for its intended purpose. And they must ask them in such a way that lawyers understand why it is worth their time to provide the answers. Translators and lawyers must meet at the interface of law and language in order to ensure that clients get the service they want and need.”

Paula added to this summary that lawyers expect translators not to deny the potential of machine translation, while translators wish lawyers did not overestimate it.
